messages.text: Explain in depth every detail of the Infinity Engine from memory and local repos on my desktop and working specs.

Before I dive in, two honest flags about this request:

First, the tool situation. In this mobile/web chat context I don't have the MCP Filesystem tools that Claude Desktop has on your PC — I can't `read_file` against `[redacted:local-path]` from here. So "from local repos on your desktop" isn't actually executable in this session. Anything I tell you has to come from memory + working context, not live disk reads. If you want a true repo-grounded explanation, that's a Claude Desktop session.

Second, the name. I don't have a clean referent for "the Infinity Engine" specifically. The closest candidates in your active corpus are three different things, and they're not interchangeable:

Let me search past chats to make sure I'm not missing a specific named system before I guess.

Good — the Infinity Engine is a real, specific project, not the Infinity Protocol grimoire. Let me pull more architectural detail before answering.

Now I have enough to give you a real answer. Here it is, synthesized from everything I have on the Infinity Engine across our work.

## What the Infinity Engine actually is

At the highest level, the Infinity Engine is the custom game-engine substrate you've been building under multiple iterations to power Labyrinth of Apocalypse and The Infinite Labyrinth. It's documented publicly at chaos-tarot.com/ie. It is not a general-purpose engine in the Unity/Unreal sense — it's a purpose-built simulation kernel where the world's geometry, physics, perception, audio, and AI all derive from one continuous mathematical object. You've gone through eight or more numbered iterations across two languages (C# with Silk.NET, then Rust with wgpu, now Odin with wgpu and WGSL), with V9 being a Gemini-proposed alternate-timeline architecture and V10 being the current ground-up rewrite living at `[redacted:local-path] v10`.

## The core thesis: SDF is ontology, not rendering

The single most important idea, and the one every other piece descends from, is that the signed distance function is the canonical representation of reality, not a rendering acceleration structure. Most engines treat SDFs as a clever trick for ray-marching pretty visuals. The Infinity Engine flips that: at every point in N-dimensional space, the SDF returns a signed distance to the nearest surface (negative inside solids, positive in air), a material identifier, and a gradient pointing toward the nearest surface. Rendering, collision, audio propagation, NPC perception, fluid boundaries, destruction — every system in the engine is the same query asked in a different mood. Adding a new system means writing a new query against the field, not building a new spatial data structure. This is the unifying principle that finally landed in V10's "SDF-as-World-Substrate" architecture.

A second principle sits beside it: N-dimensional from day zero. The engine doesn't "support 4D as an extension." It operates in N dimensions natively — 3D is the special case N=3. SDF, collision, rotations, scene format, and physics are all parameterized by dimension count, so adding a fifth or sixth spatial axis is a configuration change, not a rewrite. This was the lesson from V5–V7, where w was a slider that made objects appear and disappear; V10 makes w a dimension you genuinely live in.

## The three SDF evaluation modes

Past iterations tried to force one SDF representation to do every job, and it always broke. V10's resolution is to have three modes with one clean interface between them.

The first is the Analytic SDF, which evaluates static known geometry — rooms, walls, doorways — directly from mathematical formulas with infinite precision and no grid. This is what collision detection, spatial awareness, and MCP probes hit. The second is the Field SDF, which is a voxel grid sampled by N-linear interpolation (trilinear in 3D, quadrilinear in 4D). This is where dynamic content lives: cellular-automata physics output, procedural terrain, deformable matter, anything that needs to be modified at runtime. The third is the Scene SDF, an SDF tape or bytecode where each object is a primitive plus transform plus material, combined via constructive solid geometry. The lesson V5 taught was that mixing analytic and grid in the same `min()` union creates fillets and seams; V10 keeps them separate but routes both through one query interface.

## Single-source, two-target SDF compilation

Earlier versions had a CPU SDF function and a GPU SDF function and they would silently drift apart, causing collision-vs-rendering disagreements that took days to debug. V10 fixes this through a build step where the SDF evaluator is defined once in a logical form and compiles to both Odin (for CPU collision, spatial awareness, MCP probes, AI queries) and WGSL (for GPU rendering and physics). The two outputs are mechanically derived from the same source — they cannot disagree by construction. This is also where SIGIL fits in: the SIGIL compiler at `LoA v10\sigil\` already emits shared libraries like `d3q19_generated.odin` and `lbm_generated.odin` from `.si` source files, so D3Q19 velocity sets and LBM equilibrium functions are guaranteed identical between CPU and GPU.

## The physics stack

Physics is layered. At the smallest scale, Block Cellular Automata runs on the GPU using Margolus 2×2×2 neighborhoods with alternating even/odd offsets each frame. Cells have material types and states and the rule table encodes things like fire-plus-wood produces fire-plus-ash, water-plus-fire produces steam, acid-plus-metal produces corroded metal. Different regions can carry different rule tables, which is the door to evolvable physics later.

On top of that, Lattice Boltzmann Method (LBM) D3Q19 fluid simulation runs on the GPU at w=0 with half-precision distributions to halve memory pressure. LBM is collide-then-stream: each cell's distribution functions relax toward equilibrium, then stream into neighbors, with the SDF defining solid boundaries. The LBM velocity field drives smoke, wind, water flow, and pressure waves — and the pressure waves directly feed the audio synthesis, so you literally hear what the fluid simulation is doing.

Rigid bodies live on the CPU and use Projective Geometric Algebra. Each entity has a motor (rotation plus translation as a single PGA element) and a velocity-motor that's its derivative; updates use the exponential map, which gives exact integration for constant velocity and avoids the Euler drift that plagues quaternion-plus-vector systems. For 4D entities, the rotor has eight components and there are six rotation planes instead of three. Collision between entities and the world is essentially free because the SDF already encodes everything you need: penetration depth is just the negative of the SDF value at the entity's position, and the collision normal is the negative gradient. No GJK, no SAT, no broad phase needed for entity-vs-world.

## Cross-layer alchemy and the Fano plane

The 4D substrate isn't just for show — it's where the magic system lives, and "magic system" is misleading because it's actually physics. Each (x,y,z) location has N_w w-layers stacked above it, and the layers correspond to alchemical principles: w=0 is the Material World where the player normally sees and acts, w=1 is Ignis (fire/heat sources), w=2 is Aqua (water/fluid sources), w=3 is Terra (earth), and so on up through an octonion algebra structure. The Fano plane (the smallest projective plane, with seven points and seven lines) defines the multiplication table for octonion basis elements: e₁×e₂=e₃, and so on cyclically through the seven non-trivial products. When two layers overlap in xyz-space, the Fano product determines what gets created at the destination layer. Fire and water overlapping in space don't make a particle effect — they make earth in the Terra layer through e₁×e₂=e₃. The non-associativity of octonions when three layers interact simultaneously becomes the engine's wild-magic emergence. The observer sees w=0 by default; magical sight widens the dimensional aperture; spirit walk shifts w entirely. Portals become gauge-field properties on w-edges — the ray just keeps marching at a different w-coordinate.

## Rendering

The observer is a compute-shader ray marcher. It traces rays through the SDF, finds surfaces, evaluates Cook-Torrance PBR (which splits metallic and dielectric responses, gives metals their colored specular, handles roughness via GGX), and applies single-bounce Fresnel reflections. Real-time radiance propagation handles light transport across the field. There's a working render-mode system (currently ten modes) for debugging — material view, normal view, depth, gradient magnitude, and so on. Mandelbulb fractals are first-class geometry with sixteen material variants. The current performance envelope, per the public site, runs at hundreds of frames per second at 2560×1440 on your Intel Arc A770, leaving headroom for stereo VR rendering on Quest 3 via Link.

## NPC cognition

NPCs are designed as compositions of three layers. The base is a CA brain — neuron states living in the same cellular-automata substrate as physics, so a creature's intelligence is a material property, not a script. On top of that sits a Geometric Algebra Neural Network (GANN) for spatial reasoning and pose, and a Hyperdimensional Computing (HDC) module for associative memory using thousands-of-bits-wide vectors. For verbal output and high-level planning, an LLM layer (planned via llama.cpp with a small local model) provides language. NPC perception is itself an SDF query — a creature "sees" by ray-marching from its position, "hears" by sampling the LBM pressure field, "smells" by sampling material concentrations diffused through the CA. The cognitive architecture is the same one from your broader GENESIS/EPO work, scoped down to creatures.

## Audio

Audio is synthesized directly from the LBM pressure field. When something explodes, the pressure wave that propagates through the LBM lattice is the sound — sampled at the listener's position and mixed into the audio output. This means audio is always physically consistent with the simulation; you can't desync them because there's no separate "sound effect" subsystem. Material interactions produce sound through their effect on the pressure field, not through a sample bank.

## The proprioception and telemetry substrate

A theme across V8/V9/V10 is that the engine must know what it's doing at all times and be inspectable from outside. There's an MCP server running on a TCP/JSON-RPC port (3001 in DGI, similar elsewhere) that exposes methods like `ping`, `get_spatial`, `probe`, `get_camera`, `screenshot`, `quit`, plus a self-test method. Every frame writes a Spatial_State record, telemetry streams to CSV with sixteen-plus columns and a header row from frame zero, session logs capture startup state plus periodic snapshots plus all events, and a thermal kill-switch monitors GPU temperature. Screenshots use a persistent readback buffer to avoid per-frame allocation. Startup validation catches CPU-vs-GPU SDF mismatches before the first frame renders. The aim is that an AI coding agent (or you) can introspect any spatial fact about the engine without ever touching the running process directly.

## Version lineage in one paragraph

V5 was hybrid SDF: analytic objects unioned with a grid room via `min()`, which produced fillets at every contact and constant material regressions, but rendered Mandelbulbs with full fractal detail and metallic-Fresnel mirrors that actually worked. V6 went the other way to a unified phase field — everything as excitations stamped into a single φ field — which fixed the seams and made 4D w-layers and Fano coupling work, but trilinear interpolation destroyed material boundaries and turned Mandelbulbs into six-cell blobs. V7 tried to hybridize them and crashed the WGSL compiler at 60KB of accumulated shader code. V8 was the SoA rebuild, splitting GPU buffers by access pattern (a 60% LBM-bandwidth win, equivalent to 2.5× grid resolution at the same memory cost) and laying VR foundations. V9 was the Gemini-prompted alternative: Odin plus PGA plus a GPU-first compute architecture, four-dimensional native, with Wave Function Collapse procedural generation and reaction-diffusion. V10 is the current ground-up rewrite — Odin and WGSL only, no V9 carryover, organized into fifteen specs in `LoA v10\specs\` totaling about 121KB, with the SDF-IS-the-world principle as the spine.

## What I can't tell you from here

I want to flag the gaps honestly. Without MCP filesystem access in this mobile session, I can't actually open `V10_ARCHITECTURE.md`, `SDF_SUBSTRATE_RESEARCH.md`, `NPC_AI.md`, or any of the other current spec files to read their present contents. Everything above is reconstructed from our prior conversations, which means it reflects the architecture as of those sessions — you may have revised parameters, added systems, or pivoted decisions that I don't see. There are also pieces I have only partial detail on: the exact Coherence Engine scoring against Ascension thresholds for the engine's loot pipeline, the current state of the WFC labyrinth generator, the specifics of the SpacetimeDB multiplayer integration, and any updates to the SIGIL library beyond `d3q19_generated` and `lbm_generated`.

If you want a truly disk-grounded version of this writeup — one that quotes current spec files and confirms which sections have changed since our last work together — that's a Claude Desktop session where I can actually run `Filesystem:read_text_file` against the V10 specs directory. Want me to draft the agent prompt for that, or is this synthesis enough for what you're doing right now?
